newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Float seen best alternative for NZ's GPS property.
newsitem.headline: Float seen best alternative for NZ's GPS property.

text.p: The chairman of New Zealand's state property owning arm, Government Property Services, said on Thursday he believed a public float would yield the best returns if GPS were to become earmarked for sale.
Colin Beyer made the comment to Reuters after a review of the future of GPS by a parliamentary select committee.
"I think the method is one element, the timing is the other element. If you get the method and the timing right, probably the best method is to float the company," Beyer said.
He would not comment on the best time for such an action because the company was not officially for sale.
Asked if the board's advice to GPS's shareholding ministers would be for an eventual public float, Beyer said, "It probably would be at the current time."
But he added, "Any question of a sale has been deferred for an indeterminate period."
He said some properties were currently being sold to rationalise the portfolio.
A planned sale of the bulk of GPS properties, excluding some buildings that house key government and defence functions, was put on hold last year after prices did not meet expectations.
Market sources said an offer for the full portfolio had been rejected by government just before the October election.
In March Finance Minister Bill Birch, whose ministry is one of the shareholders in GPS, said government planned to continue to sell GPS properties.

"The coalition govenment doesn't think the ownership of commercial buildings is part of the strategic role of government. It is a collection of buildings. We will work to eventually reduce the ownership of the buildings which we don't think are strategic," Birch said.
"We think the money is better off in debt repayment, quite frankly."
GPS's statement of corporate intent shows directors valued the company at $162 million at March 31, 1996.
"Since 1996 we have had a modest increase in valuations of our properties," Beyer told the select committee.
"I am satisfied the market is now on the up, but how long that will continue is anyone's guess," Beyer said.

He said the current market value of Bowen House, which houses parliamentarians who cannot be accommodated in the main Wellington parliamentary complex, was $38 million and the annual rent on the building was about $4 million.
The government has said it wants to go ahead with a new $94 million building for cabinet ministers despite a 200,000 signature petition delivered this week opposing the plan.
